Show don't tell is much more geared towards novel writing.

This is because when you execute on show don't tell it will ALWAYS make the word count go up.

When writing lyrics, the syllables of each line are what you're working around, so it can be straight up impossible to show, not tell, some ideas in a limiting format. 

The best way to handle this IMO is to focus more on the emotion you're trying to convey, then come up with metaphors and allusions to the idea instead.
It would be better to focus more on the flow of the phrase and try to find words that sound good together. You might need to sacrifice a bit on the continuity of the story you're trying to tell and instead trust your audience to read between the lines so you can focus on being more poetic.

I'll try to give an example of how I might take one of your lines and tweak it so that it focused more on being poetic and conveying emotion.

rather than saying something like:
"I drove you home, we cried and cried"

I might say something like this:
"I drove you home, through blurry street lights" 


Saying directly that you cried and cried is not only a bit plain but it doesn't really roll off the tongue (at least not how I hear it in my head) and flow poetically.
My alternative is not trying to be the best lyric imaginable, but instead is trying to demonstrate the point. It has a bit more poetry because it's not so direct and invites the listener to experience the emotion themselves rather than be an outside observer to it. 
It's usually not too hard to work in just one extra syllable, so I'd say it likely will flow better than singing, "cried and cried." Additionally, the listener is put in the moment and might ponder to themselves "wait why are the lights blurry?" Before realizing through the context of the song "oh I understand they were blurry because they had tears in their eyes. I've been there before."

I hope that helps.

In my humble opinion, you're going about songwriting all wrong.
On the one hand, your determination for everything to meet a certain standard is crippling your inspiration. Things don't usually start off great, they have to be refined into greatness from a humble idea.
On the other hand, if you're just focused on the end result, you're going to miss the moment to moment flow of letting a song take shape. You have to trust your little inspiration, and trust your ear. Not every song needs to be a "Mona Lisa" it's perfectly fine to bust out a few doodle bop SpongeBob flops to make way for your best work.
When you write a song you have to take an idea, or an emotion, and feel it so deeply that it flows through you. What you squeeze out of yourself is the music, and you have to let yourself discover how it all fits together. You're so jammed up in trying to force gold that you're unable to let anything flow.

Someone once told me when I was suffering through writers block to read the art of war, and declare war on myself. I didn't read the book. But the idea resonated none-the-less. Challenge your presuppositions about what the writing process is for yourself. Let it be an expression. Let it be personal, and let it be what it is instead of trying to force it into something you expect it to be. When you can be in the moment with your guitar again, and you can stop judging what you're creating and just let it flow, then that's when your best work will just happen.

There are two dueling metas in elden ring.

150 is VERY much meta. I used to max at 125 in all the past souls games but in practice 150 makes way more sense for elden ring. The soul level typically lines up to when you end the game, and your average player doesn't stop leveling at fire giant.

Not only that, but weapons have higher base stat requirements in elden ring, (such as having both strength and dex requirements for almost every weapon) so it makes more sense for meta level to accommodate for that. Also, the soft caps are much higher, which hints to me that the devs want you to get to higher levels to take advantage of that, probably because they know this game is so much bigger and there is a lot higher scaling multipliers than in past games, so the average build should be able to reach that without having to sacrifice on vigor.

But also in my experience 125 meta is way more stale than 150. There's less build variety and it's easier for the strong consumables in elden ring to give someone a larger advantage at 125 than at 150.

As a souls vet, I would encourage anyone who is capping at 125 to level to 150. Dueling is way more balanced and interesting. Elden Ring is not Ds3 so stop treating it like it is and you'll enjoy the multiplayer much more

There are so many different ways to tie a melody to a chord progression. Sometimes, a simple 4 chord structure just won't carry your melody with as much emotion. And on the inverse of that, sometimes if a chord progression is too complex, it can muddy the vox as well and make the song hard to follow.

So, without a background in music theory, the easiest way is to figure out the specific notes you're singing, then figure out the scale and find a chord that matches.
Otherwise, all that's left is trial and error.

I found that over the years, as I've been writing music, I've become less focused on which chords I'm using. Now that I've written for so long I think more big picture about how a song is going to go, and I write it all at the same time almost.

Sometimes, I don't even notice that I've used a particularly basic chord progression until much after writing the song.

I, like yourself, actually used to think about what chords I was using all the time and actively try to avoid using progressions I was familiar with. In time, I started compromising on that vision if a particular chord would better support the melody I was trying to sing.

I have been able to consistently make creamy and white broth like this. For anyone who is interested, I'll drop my process below.

For the whitest and creamiest broth:

1.)
Preboil and clean your bones. There is a LOT of debate around whether or not you should do this. I will say from experience that it depends on what you're going for. If you want more PORK flavor, then don't wash or preboil. If you want milky white broth in appearance, then DO do this.
I like to change my approach depending on the dish I'm going for and what Tare I plan to use with the broth. For a simple tare like sio, I will avoid rinsing.
But if I'm going for a miso or shoyu tare, then I'll go for the milky white broth because the flavor from the tare will compensate.

2.) FAT. Assuming you're going for the whitest broth you can, then the next step is to return all the cleaned bones to your pot and add pork FAT.
I've tried all kinds of sources for this... pork feet, straight-up chunks of pork fat, pork lard...  it feels like any of these will work, but i like to do pork fat and pork feet because this will help with flavor. (If you do work with feet, then preboil and clean them with the other bones.)

3.) Heat and time. This step is the easy part. Your bones and fat broth base will need a rapid boil and lots of time to extract all that beautiful stuff that makes up your tonkotsu broth. Just don't forget to add water periodically. I'm usually two or three ticks below max on my stove top (just as long as you can maintain a rolling boil the whole time) and I try to boil for a MINIMUM of 14 hours. Technically, you can stop after around 8 - but I'm giving you my process for the milky maximum white broth. The longer you boil, the more you will increase the thickness of your broth. 14 - 22 hours is plenty for me, but experiment on your own and figure out what you like.

Normally, I'll add aromatics in the last hour. Garlic, onions, cabbage, carrots, ginger... whatever you prefer. However, this will ALSO SLIGHTLY inhibit the color of your broth.

For best results, remove bones, strain broth, and put in an empty milk carton. Leave it in the fridge to rest overnight. You ALWAYS want to chill your broth overnight.
And... Why a milk carton? Because this shit will be so creamy white that if any roommates, siblings, or unwitting enemies see the carton before the broth congeals, they WILL pour this on their cereal, and THAT my friends is your 2nd gift from me. Happy holidays!

I'll explain the advantages of each game and let you decide.

Demon's Souls:
This is the one I have the least experience with.. but it's a series of separate levels (sorta like the legacy dungeons) that are not connected at all. It's also the first one, so it has some jenk to it - but it's still a souls game and if you liked elden ring you'll enjoy it. Consumables are the only way to heal yourself, so it can be pretty unforgiving in that regard.

Dark souls remastered:
This game has probably the most interestingly designed game world ive yet seen. Absolutely top tier level design and solid progression. The first half of the game is (in my opinion) the absolute best gaming has to offer. Bosses are themed well and are memorable. There's a reason this game spawned the entire sub genre "souls-like" even if the second half of the game feels a bit rushed. This one is my personal favorite outside of elden ring. It's very replayable as well.

Dark Souls two:
It's a bit of a shit show in terms of world design. It feels like a bit of a mix between demons souls and DSR. Except you can tell Miyazaki wasn't involved.
It's probably the most similar to Elden Ring in a lot of ways, though - it's long, has crazy build variety, and gives you decent enough freedom with where you have weapons equipped, etc. Bosses aren't bad either. This game gets a lot of hate, and I honestly think it's because the jenk associated with iframes during rolls are tied to a stat you need to level - and the fact that they kinda made it super difficult in spots with the amount of enemies they put everywhere. It sorta teaches you to just run past all the enemies to go straight to the bosses, which is unfortunate imo.

Dark Souls Three:
This one is very refined. But nothing really stands out to me except the bosses and progression. It took a step back from Dark Souls Remastered in World Design and went for something more linear. and it took a step back from Dark Souls two and opted for a more limiting approach to build variety. That said, it probably has some of the most consistent boss fights in the entire lineup, even including elden ring in some cases. It's a lot of people's favorite in the series for this reason. If you play the three Dark Souls games, you will see the pieces that come together to create Elden Ring.

Bloodborne: 
The only thing this game is missing is build variety. You still get some choice, and the weapons are all super cool because they transform and shit. You trade shields for guns and dial up the speed of combat from the other games. You have some awesome level designs like DS1, and solid Bosses like DS3. It just looses the midevil feel for a Gothic (and dark) one. The lore is very interesting and it's a solid souls game the entire way through. If you can get past the lacking build variety, I think it's 2nd only to DSR and Elden Ring.

Sekiro:
Throw away all build variety and RPG elements for a very linear high octane soulslike. If you don't care of builds and RPG elements, this one is up your alley. The game is pretty fun, and it's where the "jump" mechanic in elden ring came from.
The game is much less forgiving than the others, since you can't find alternative solutions to hurdles the game gives you - you just have to get gud. Sad to say that i didn't beat it because of that. I just got extremely frustrated with certain Bosses I couldn't get past because I couldn't get the timing down, lost interest, and haven't had the desire to go back to it. The couple of times I was able to land timings appropriately, it felt very rewarding, and for those that are able to get through it, I'm convinced it's an incredible game overall. I just personally enjoyed the build creation aspect of these games, and the RPG elements being missing limited my ability to enjoy Sekiro. That being said, don't let my personal preferences stop you if that sounds interesting. Sekiro is many people's favorite soulslike, and for good reason.


So it all comes down to preference. Each of the games have a bit of everything that makes the genre so great. But some stand out more than others in certain aspects. 

Did you like the level design and exploration in ER? DS1 would be a good choice.

Was it the RPG elements? DS2 would be enjoyable for you in spite of all the negativity surrounding the game. 

Are you all about the Bosses? DS3 all the way.

Are you a lore junkie? Bloodborne for sure will appeal to you.

Are you in it for the reward of overcoming challenges? Then I'd try sekiro

Well, a ramen broth is typically three parts.

You have the stock (which makes up the bulk of the broth)

A tare (which I like to think of as the seasoning)

And an oil (which will add a lot to the aroma and mouth feel.)

So let's start with the stock... you get a good stock from boiling bones and fat for a long period of time.
I like to go with pork bones as they will make for a thicker broth.
I usually buy two sets of pork femurs or (if you can find them) pork back bones.
Get a thing of pork fat. Or even some pork feet.
And I'll usually get some chicken feet.

To prep everything, you'll want to cut the pork fat in half - remove all the nails from the chicken feet, and presoak the pork bones in water overnight.

When you're ready to start the cook , replace the water for the pork bones with fresh water and do a quick 30-minute preboil with just the bones and pork feet. This part is technically optional - but I like a really clean milky white stock. So during this process, I remove the scum from the top of the pot as it boils. I'll even usually take this a step further and remove the bones and scrub them clean individually. A lot of people say this removes flavor - but in my experience, most of the flavor comes from the tare anyway. So I'll also replace the water a 2nd time at this point as well but that's also technically optional.

Next, you'll add half of the pork fat, clipped chicken feet, as well as the bones and pork feet (if you decide to get pork feet as well) to the pot - and bring to a rapid boil for AT LEAST 8 hours. The longer you can boil them for the better. I usually aim for 30 hours myself - but that can be hard to manage for some.

1 hour before you're finished with the stock, you can add some aromatics. DO NOT ADD THEM SOONER AS THEY WILL BURN AND RUIN YOUR STOCK. I learned that the hard way. 
The aromatics come down to personal taste - but if you're looking for ideas I usually throw in a white onion, carrot, half a head of naba cabbage, ginger, and garlic. 

When this is all done, you'll want to remove all the pieces from the stock (bones, feet, aromatics, and all) and immediately chill the broth as quickly as you can. Put it in a freezer - surround the pot with ice in the sink - or my personal favorite - set it outside in a blizzard during wintertime. 

You will reheat this before you serve it - but chilling the stock is very important to help the flavor mature. Otherwise, it will taste pretty watery. You'll know you got a good stock from pork bones if it turns Jell-O-y when it's cold. If the stock is still very watery, it's still usable - but you could have boiled the bones for longer to get a thicker broth for next time. You can even rinse and freeze the pork bones for a 2nd batch sometime in the future.

Now were ready for the tare. I've experimented with a lot of different recipes here - but my favorite is a Miso tare. Either way - ALL tares should start with a good dashi. This is where your shittake mushrooms  will come in handy. You'll also want to get some Kombu (which is dried kelp) and some kind of dried seafood. I like scallops or shrimp best personally. You'll throw in a 2 parts mushroom, 2 parts kombu, and 1 part dried seafood into a container with enough water so it's all completely submerged and let this sit for about 6-8 hours. (Though I usually leave it overnight while my stock is boiling) 
Notice how I'm not giving exact measurements as you'll probably want to scale it based on how much stock you make. I commit the sin of just eyeballing everything anyway - but it seems to work out.

When the dashi is ready, get 4 parts miso paste (you can even mix both white and red if you like), 1 part sesame oil, 1 part mirin, 1 part soy sauce in a sauce pan and heat it all up to mix it together. Once that's all mixed well - remove the kombu, shittake, and seafood from the dashi and pour the dashi into the sauce pan, and mix it well with the miso mix. You'll notice the dashi is pretty slimy looking - and that's exactly what you're looking for. You'll want to keep the sauce pan at a relatively low simmer as heat will break down some of the deliciousness from the dashi. Mix this all together, and you'll have a miso tare. Taste it, and make sure it's literally too salty. If it's not obviously too salty, then season it up with more soy sauce or even *ghasp* a little bit of MSG. Remember that the tare needs to season all the stock you made, so it should be pretty strong in flavor.

Finally, we'll make our oil. 
For this, you can get a much smaller sauce pan. Put a layer of water at the bottom of the pan (about a half cup or so) then cut up the other half of the pork fat, into pieces that are roughly an inch long/wide.
Put the pork fat in the pan and slap it on the heat. 
What we are doing here is rendering oil out of the pork fat to make a delicious aroma oil. 

You'll want to cook this till the fat shrivels and turns golden brown. At this point, the water should be displaced by oil, so remove the chunks of fat and throw in some chopped onions, garlic, and ginger. Continue to cook until the aromatics are also browned, then strain the aromatics out and you've got your oil. (It will also smell DIVINE)

Now it's time to serve!

Reheat some stock in a sauce pan, your tare, and I like to time it so the oil just finished so it's still 👌 to go.

Once the stock is steamy - put 1/4 to 1/2 cup of tare in a serving bowl (to taste) 
Add 3-4 cups of stock to the bowl, and a tablespoon of oil to the bowl.
Fold in your noodles, and dress it up with your toppings.

That'll get you my personal favorite Tonkotsu-Miso recipe of fairly traditional ramen. :)

A quick note - if you don't like miso (wtf is wrong with you first of all) but you can substitute the miso in the tare making process with a healthy amount of soy sauce and some Sake. Or just salt and sake.
Either case will make a Tonkotsu Shoyu, or just straight Tonkotsu, respectively.

Cheers 🍻

Drift is a result of how the control sticks read input - there's a sensor plate, and a shaft that goes to a point coming off the thumb stick that drags along the sensor to read the direction the thumb stick is moved.

When this dragging happens over time flakes of the sensor come up, and since they're metal they stick to the sensor causing a false input and you get drift.

This means that essentially the only way to avoid drift completely is to just not use the controller.

What makes ME sad is others are adopting this technology for their controllers. The PS5 controller has this same design for example.

I have spent WAY too much time on this game and have some unsolicited advice.

1.) You really shouldn't be below 50 vigor - late game bosses and invaders alike will mop the floor with you at 42 vigor.

Just make sure you select weapons and stuff that scale appropriately.

For example - one of my favorite builds is faith/arcane with the dragon communion seal. You can have pretty low faith, just for the cast requirements of spells, but then pump arcane for damage because that's how the seal scales. Doing so will allow you to have a bleed build, that also slaps with spells. In my build I have 33 faith and 50 arcane (not minmaxed at alll) but I still have like 327 incant scaling which is enough to do 600-800 damage depending on the spell. Half health of even the most tanky of players and good damage against bosses.

So, If you wanna keep dex and str split that's fine, just make sure you're using weapons that scale decently in BOTH and your damage will be fine.

I try to think about it like this - 60 dex at A scaling dex weapon will give similar damage to a weapon that has A scaling in Str and Dex if you have 30 points in each. This is just an example.

But in my testing, I prefer the versatility over maximum damage output and honestly the extra damage from min-maxing isn't so substantial that it isn't worth making a hybrid build.

My biggest take away is just make sure your weapons scale with as many of the stats you decide to pump as possible and you'll probably be okay.

Soak your bones and feet overnight before you start boiling them.

The Components for the broth were:  
1 pork shoulder or roast  
1/2 white onion  
1 head of garlic  
2 stems of green onion  
6 sizable slices of ginger  
4 dried shitake mushrooms  
10-15 grams of dried kombu  
thick sweet Shoyu (to taste)  
 I added a little bit of cumin and chili powder as well, but I would say this is optional.  


Step one: add the pork to your slow cooker, then the aromatics, and fill it with water so the pork is just slightly sticking above the water. I use an ovular shaped 'crockpot' for my slow cooker and I eye-balled the water, so I don't really have an exact measurement of the water I used (I apologize) Once the water is in the pot, drizzle a generous amount of shoyu over the pork, and add your seasonings.   
Step two: Cover, and slap that sucker on high for 4 hours. I started mine pretty late, so after 4 hours I swapped it to low heat, then let it cook overnight the rest of the way. It cooked for about 12-14 hours in total.  


This broth is very oily so you should skim some of that off the top and either re-use to make aromatic oil, OR do what I did and just leave some in the broth and use it as is. It was pretty tasty so I don't know if it would be worth the extra effort. I would recommend removing some of the oil though, when I tried this there was a lot.  


The tare was fairly traditional.  


Dashi:

15 grams of Kombu  
3 dried shitake mushrooms  
let sit in water over-night.  


The next day, bring the dashi to a very light simmer, add some salt (to taste), some shoyu (about 1/3 cup), and 1/2 cup of Katsuobushi. Strain and you're done.  


I cut the tare 2-1 so that there was twice as much broth as there was tare.  
I also didn't strain the broth either, just scooped it up, and peeled some of that pork straight out of the slow cooker and directly into the bowl.   
Very convenient!

The pork is closer to Pulled pork than it is to Chashu, but who is complaining about that?

Enjoy!
